title.value: Further clarification via ablation studies and t-SNE analysis

comment.value:
# Weaknesses 
 
1. While the paper thoroughly describes the TDA pipeline, it lacks mathematical or conceptual explanation of why these topological features are so discriminative for 3D object recognition. Suggest including an analysis of feature distribution (e.g., t-SNE visualization or correlation between persistence features and class separability) to reveal interpretability and rationale. 

- We now include a t-SNE analysis (Fig. 10 and before the conclusion) showing that the pre-computed topological descriptors can form clearly separated, class-consistent clusters via the CNN, demonstrating that these features naturally encode discriminative topological signatures and providing the conceptual rationale. 

 
 
2. The model uses 57 manually chosen filtrations with fixed parameters (e.g., voxel size 0.05, r=1 for density). This extensive manual setup may limit adaptability.  

 - Thank you for raising this concern. The parameters have worked extremely effectively on different kinds of datasets, such as VesselMNIST3D, AdrenalMNIST3D, ModelNet, ScanObjectNN, and OmniObject3D. So, we believe our method is adaptable to different types of datasets. 

 
3. The paper claims new SOTA performance, but comparisons might not be fair since TACO-Net uses voxelized inputs while many baselines use raw point clouds or multi-view images. 
 
- It is standard to compare all types of existing techniques for ModelNet – even Princeton maintains such a generalized list. One can pick any paper and see that, so we just followed the practice.  
Our claim of SOTA is made under the standard ModelNet protocol, where most methods, including multi-view and voxel-based approaches, assume canonical orientation. To ensure fairness, we compared against leading point-based and multi-view baselines under the same train/test split. Furthermore, we validated TACO-Net on OmniObject3D and ScanObjectNN, which lack canonical alignment, achieving competitive or SOTA performance. These results indicate that improvements stem from the proposed topological descriptors and the learning of them thereafter rather than voxelization alone. Note that VoxNet and 3DShapeNet (which we compare against) also use voxelized inputs, but do not achieve this high accuracy across numerous datasets. 
 
# Questions 
 
1. How sensitive is TACO-Net’s performance to voxel size, number of filtrations, or noise level? Could these hyperparameters be learned dynamically?  

- We thank the reviewer for raising this point. Our experiments (Sec. 3.1, Fig. 8(a), Tables 3 and 10) show that TACO-Net’s accuracy is moderately sensitive to voxel size and filtration count: OA varies by ~0.7% across voxel sizes 0.03 - 0.07 and between ~80 - 98% across filtration (except the erosion only case) subsets (Table 3). Robustness to noise is strong under normal-level corruption but degrades under extreme distortions, as expected. Further, we show in the revised version that our method’s performance surpasses the recent seminal supervised learning only methods, such as PointNext and PointMLP, for the hardest variant of the challenging ScanObjectNN dataset, without any hyperparameter tuning specific to this dataset. Learning these parameters might be possible, but that remains a future avenue to explore.

 
2. Have the authors tried integrating topological features directly into a neural network (e.g., using persistent homology layers) instead of precomputing them? 
 
- We appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion. In the current work, we did not explore integrating persistent homology or topological features as differentiable layers within the network. Our focus was on demonstrating that computed but not learned topological descriptors, when combined with a lightweight CNN, can achieve state-of-the-art accuracy and robustness. We agree that end-to-end differentiable TDA is an exciting and new direction, and we will consider it a key avenue for future work. That said, we did a pilot study with the PersLay layer, in which case we failed to achieve any reasonable result.

summary.value:
1．	This paper presents TACO-Net, a novel framework for 3D object classification that leverages Topological Data Analysis (TDA) through cubical persistence. 
2．	The method converts point clouds into 3D binary images, applies a diverse set of 57 filtrations to generate grayscale images, extracts topological feature vectors from their persistence diagrams, and classifies these vectors using a lightweight 1D CNN. 
3．	The authors demonstrate state-of-the-art (SOTA) or highly competitive results on multiple benchmarks, including ModelNet, real-world datasets (OmniObject3D, ScanObjectNN), and medical imaging datasets.

strengths.value:
1. The core strength of this work is its innovative application of TDA. The move away from standard deep learning architectures on raw points/voxels/views to a topology-first approach is a significant and refreshing contribution to the field.
2.  The results are impressive. Achieving SOTA accuracy on the highly competitive ModelNet10 and ModelNet40 benchmarks  is a remarkable feat that strongly validates the proposed method. Achieving SOTA on these canonical benchmarks is a clear indicator of a powerful new approach.
3.  The paper thoroughly demonstrates the generalizability of TACO-Net across diverse data domains.
4.  The experimental section is extensive and rigorous. The inclusion of shape retrieval results, an ablation study, comparisons with non-deep learning methods (XGBoost, Random Forest), and a parameter efficiency analysis provides a very complete picture of the method's capabilities and justifies the design choices.
5. The paper provides a theoretical time complexity analysis for the pipeline adds rigor. The discussion on the trade-offs between feature vector length, voxel size, and accuracy is practical and useful for future researchers or practitioners looking to adapt this work.

weaknesses.value:
1.  This is the most significant weakness of the proposed pipeline. A feature generation throughput is prohibitively slow for any real-time application. While the 1D CNN inference is fast, the TDA feature extraction is a major bottleneck. The paper acknowledges this and suggests future work on GPU acceleration, but this currently limits the practical applicability.
2.  While the ablation study on feature sets and network layers is good, it could be deepened. A more granular ablation analyzing the individual contribution of each of the six filtration types (or at least groups like the four DEDS filters) would provide clearer insight into which filtrations are most critical for the performance gains. The current study combines DEDS, making it hard to discern the value of, for example, density filtration versus erosion filtration.
3. The comparison tables are comprehensive but could be updated with a few more recent, high-performing baselines on ModelNet40 to further solidify the SOTA claim. However, the results presented are already highly competitive.

summary.value: TACO-Net is a novel SOTA framework for 3D object classification that tackles challenges in unordered and noisy point clouds by integrating Topological Data Analysis (TDA) with image filtrations. TACO-Net transforms a point cloud into a voxelized 3D image and extracts topological signatures via cubical persistence across 57 filtrations (e.g., height, radial, density). These signatures are converted into feature vectors (up to 2052 dimensions) and classified using a lightweight 1D CNN. TACO-Net achieves record accuracies of 99.05% on ModelNet40 and 99.52% on ModelNet10, while also excelling on OmniObject3D and 3D medical datasets, maintaining robustness and efficiency with only 0.72M parameters.

strengths.value:
+ TACO-Net is robust with several low perturbations (Table 8).
+ TACO-Net is a very lightweight network with only 0.72 million parameters.
+ TACO-Net achieves SOTA results on 3D object classification on ModelNet40 and ModelNet10 datasets.
+ TACO-Net achieves a new SOTA retrieval performance with a mean average precision (mAP) of 99.33 on ModelNet40.
+ The proposed model also achieves excellent results on VesselMNIST3D and AdrenalMNIST3D datasets.
+ The paper is well-written and easy to follow.

summary.value: This paper introduces a 3D object classification framework that combines topological data analysis with a 1D CNN. Each point cloud is voxelized, transformed via 57 different filtrations (height, radial, density, dilation, erosion, signed distance), and then processed through cubical persistence to obtain numerical descriptors such as persistent entropy and amplitude metrics. These handcrafted 2052-D topological features are then classified by a small 1D CNN. The method reports exceptionally high performance on several benchmarks.

strengths.value:
(1) The integration of topology and learning is interesting. The use of cubical persistence and multi-filtration topological signatures for 3D object recognition is rarely explored in 3D deep learning.

(2) The reported results outperform the existing baselines, with robustness and cross-dataset generalization demonstrated.

(3) The pipeline is well explained, mathematically grounded, and reproducible.

weaknesses.value:
(1) My main concern is the unfair comparison with the learning-based methods. The entire pipeline relies on handcrafted topological features rather than learnable representations. Every voxelization step, filtration direction, and persistence descriptor is manually designed and fixed before training. The CNN merely acts as a shallow classifier on pre-extracted features. This is not the purpose of conference like ICLR, where they prefer learning methods to replace such heavy manual engineering through representation learning. Thus, comparing TACO-Net’s performance against end-to-end learning models like PointNet, DGCNN, or PointMamba is unfair. Those methods avoid feature engineering to achieve scalability and generalization, whereas TACO-Net depends on it.

(2) There is no gradient path from the classification loss back to voxelization or TDA computations. Persistent homology, entropy, and amplitude are computed once and never updated. As a result, the model cannot adapt its topological features to the task or data distribution. In ICLR’s context, this makes the contribution engineering-oriented rather than a learning advance. Existing differentiable TDA frameworks (e.g., differentiable persistence, learnable filtrations) are not included in the comparisons. Meanwhile, although the authors cite the stability and injectivity of persistent homology, it never formalizes how these properties translate into better generalization or robustness in learning. No theoretical or empirical analysis connects topological distance metrics to classification margin, robustness, or invariance.

(3) The paper reports significant improvements on ModelNet40 and ModelNet10 using fixed voxel grids. However, voxelization implicitly aligns shapes and removes rotation/scale variance, which provides very strong priors unavailable to learning-based methods. Moreover, parameters such as voxel size and filtration selection were tuned for maximum test accuracy, which risks test-set overfitting. No cross-dataset or statistical variance analyses are presented. Therefore, the 99 % results likely reflect dataset bias and preprocessing effects rather than the contributions of the proposed topological descriptors.

(4) Computing 57 filtrations and persistent homologies per sample is extremely expensive in voxel count. While the 1D CNN itself is small, the preprocessing cost dominates the runtime, making the method impractical for large-scale or real-time applications such as robotics or autonomous driving.

questions.value:
(1) If the feature pipeline is manually engineered, what exactly is learned by TACO-Net beyond a linear/nonlinear classifier on hand-crafted descriptors?

(2) Why name the framework a “network” when no gradient flows through the voxelization, filtrations, or persistence computations?

(3) Would the same level of accuracy be achieved if you replaced the 1D CNN with a simple logistic regression or XGBoost classifier?

(4) How are the voxel grid origin, alignment, and orientation chosen? If they are globally consistent across training and test data, your pipeline benefits from pose priors that invalidate comparison with rotation-invariant baselines.

1. The process of selecting the optimal number of radial filtrations (18 for ModelNet40, 14 for AdrenalMNIST, etc.) appears to be empirical, based on a search over feature vector length. - We acknowledge that the choice of radial filtration count appears empirical. Radial filtrations capture interior organization by measuring distances from multiple reference points arranged in a 3×3×3 lattice (Fig. 3). Using all 27 centers increases dimensionality without proportional accuracy gains because many centers are highly correlated. For this reason, we empirically use the minimum number of radial filtrations that yield the highest OA.

- Yes, this step is skipped since the input is already a voxelized 3D image. It is also mentioned in Sec. 4.3.1.: “Therefore, our starting point is 3D binary images instead of point clouds for AdrenalMNIST3D and VesselMNIST3D.”

summary.value: This paper proposes TACO-Net, a 3D object classification framework that combines voxelization, multi-filtration Topological Data Analysis (TDA) via cubical persistence, and a lightweight 1D CNN classifier. The method achieves very strong empirical performance, including state-of-the-art or near state-of-the-art results on ModelNet10/40, multiple ScanObjectNN variants, OmniObject3D, 3DGrocery100, and medical datasets. Reviewers broadly agreed that the experimental validation is extensive and that the integration of TDA into 3D recognition is interesting and relatively underexplored. However, concerns were raised about the nature of the contribution relative to learning-based methods, the heavy reliance on fixed, hand-engineered feature pipelines, computational cost, and the clarity of the paper’s core message.

reviewer_concerns.value:
The rebuttal successfully addressed many technical and presentation-level concerns. The authors clarified the number of input points used across datasets, added results on all six ScanObjectNN variants and 3DGrocery100, included t-SNE visualizations to demonstrate feature discriminability, expanded ablations over filtrations, and updated comparisons with more recent baselines. Importantly, the authors clarified that the proposed topological feature extraction pipeline is largely universal across datasets, requiring minimal dataset-specific tuning—an explanation that convinced at least one initially skeptical reviewer and led them to raise their score.

Nevertheless, fundamental concerns remain. Multiple reviewers questioned whether the contribution aligns well with the learning-centric focus of the venue, as the pipeline relies heavily on non-learned, manually designed voxelization and topological feature extraction, with no gradient flow through the TDA stages.

title.value: Why the topological signatures and the CNN - are both important

comment.value:
# Weaknesses  

1. We appreciate the reviewer’s concern. Although TACO-Net uses fixed topological signatures rather than learning from raw points, the comparison is still fair because all methods tackle the same 3D classification benchmarks, and the literature routinely contrasts handcrafted feature pipelines with end-to-end models to assess trade-offs. Our core contribution is to show that these TDA descriptors, when paired with our lightweight 1D CNN, yield state-of-the-art accuracy and robustness, often surpassing far heavier deep architectures, demonstrating that well-designed topological features can rival learned representations in practice. Importantly, Tables 7 and 11 show that the handcrafted features alone are insufficient: XGBoost performs poorly, whereas our CNN learns highly discriminative representations, aligning with ICLR’s emphasis on representation learning and underscoring that the learning component of TACO-Net is essential rather than superficial.

 2. While the voxelization and TDA stages are non-learned, our aim is to demonstrate that these task-agnostic topological signatures already encode highly discriminative geometric structure, validated by the t-SNE analysis in Fig. 10, which shows clear class-wise separation derived solely from these descriptors. The stability and injectivity of persistent homology provide the theoretical basis for this discriminative behavior, and our strong results across diverse datasets further confirm their robustness and generalizability. Our contribution is orthogonal to differentiable-TDA work: rather than learning filtrations, we show that well-designed cubical filtrations produce embeddings that a lightweight CNN can effectively refine. Finally, Tables 7 and 11 demonstrate that the features alone are insufficient (XGBoost performs poorly), whereas our 1D CNN learns powerful representations from these signatures, aligning with ICLR’s emphasis on representation learning and highlighting that TACO-Net’s novelty lies in both its topological foundations and its learning architecture.
 
3. Voxelization is a standard preprocessing step in literature (e.g., VoxNet, 3DShapeNets) and is used here solely to enable cubical persistence - not to exploit alignment priors. Crucially, our strong performance extends far beyond ModelNet: we achieve high accuracy on OmniObject3D, six ScanObjectNN variants, and two medical datasets, none of which provide canonical alignment, demonstrating that our gains are not tied to ModelNet-specific biases. To mitigate concerns about overfitting, we report averages over five runs and show robustness under severe corruptions (ModelNet40-C). Taken together, these results indicate that TACO-Net’s improvements arise from the proposed topological descriptors and not from voxelization artifacts or dataset priors.  
 
4. We agree that the filtrations dominate computation, and accelerating this step, e.g., via GPU integration, is a priority for future work. Still, this paper is the first to show that TDA can deliver competitive or state-of-the-art results on multiple challenging real-world datasets, establishing a strong foundation for more efficient TDA-based pipelines in robotics and vision.
 
# Questions 
 
1. While the topological descriptors are hand-engineered, they do not by themselves encode class-specific structure. TACO-Net’s 1D CNN learns nonlinear interactions across topological signatures, enabling discriminative patterns that simple classifiers cannot capture. This is supported by our ablations and comparisons: XGBoost and Random Forest underperform by up to ~30% (Tables 7 & 11), and replacing our CNN with a heavier transformer yields only 62% accuracy, showing that our network is specifically effective at learning from these descriptors. Thus, TACO-Net is not a linear classifier on handcrafted features but a learned model that extracts meaningful higher-order topological relationships essential for its SOTA performance.

2. We use the term network because it contains a fully learnable 1D CNN that refines the topological descriptors into discriminative representations, something non-network models cannot achieve. Although the TDA stage is fixed, the CNN is a trainable neural module, justifying the naming. That said, we are open to renaming if the reviewers consider it essential.

3. When we replaced the CNN with XGBoost, accuracy dropped by ~18% for ModelNet40 and ~30% for ScanObjectNN.  

4. Our voxel grids are built per shape from its own axis-aligned bounding box (AABB), with no global alignment, rotation normalization, or dataset-level orientation assumptions. This matches the standard ModelNet protocol used by all baselines, ensuring fair comparison. We also tested rotation and shear corruptions (Table 10) and showed that performance recovers with simple augmentation. Moreover, strong results on OmniObject3D and ScanObjectNN, datasets without canonical orientations, confirm that TACO-Net does not rely on alignment priors.

Yes, you are absolutely correct. The proposed framework only needs voxelization as a pre-processing step (widely popular in this domain) that generates a 3D voxelized binary image. The entire data pre-processing and the TDA pipeline are the same for any point cloud regardless of which dataset it is coming from (illustration in Fig. 5). Thus, it does not require heavy manual parameter tuning per dataset. As per your suggestion, we will make this clear further in the final version of the paper. Thanks for your constructive comment.
